title: Why iOS feels so smooth - Act 1: The feeling

music.note: restrained tech-film score (sound_design.py music_tech_film); the old bed was 'E major' corporate pop

facts_checked_2026_11_26.render_loop: Apple tech talk 10855 'Explore UI animation hitches and the render loop' (developer.apple.com/videos/play/tech-talks/10855): event -> commit (app process) -> render prepare + render execute (render server process, GPU) -> display; every phase's deadline is the next VSYNC; a hitch = a frame that is not ready in time. 120 Hz -> 1000/120 = 8.33 ms per frame; 120 x 60 = 7,200 frames a minute.
facts_checked_2026_11_26.promotion: apple.com iPhone 18 Pro tech specs: ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz, Always-On display. Apple publishes no refresh floor - the script says 'slows right down', no number.
facts_checked_2026_11_26.rd: Apple Q4 FY2026 results (fiscal year ended 26 Sep 2026): research and development $45,765 million, up from $34,550 million (MacRumors 3 Nov 2026, MacDailyNews 3 Nov 2026). 45.77 bn / 365 = $125 million a day.
facts_checked_2026_11_26.history: P.A. Semi bought April 2008 for $278 million (Wikipedia 'Mac transition to Apple silicon', AppleInsider history of Apple silicon). A4: 2010, first Apple-designed system on a chip (iPad, then iPhone 4), made by Samsung at 45 nm. A7: Sept 2013, first 64-bit chip in a smartphone (iPhone 5s). A11 Bionic: Sept 2017, first Neural Engine. M1: Nov 2020, first Apple silicon Macs. C1 modem: Feb 2025 (iPhone 16e). N1 wireless chip: Sept 2025 (iPhone 17 line). A20 Pro: Sept 2026, iPhone 18 Pro, first iPhone chip on TSMC 2 nm (Wikipedia 'Apple A20 Pro'; TechInsights teardown via TechTimes 23 Sep 2026). 2008 -> 2026 = 18 years.

scenes.text: Watch this scroll. One frame just arrived 8 milliseconds late. You can't see it. But your thumb can feel it. On an iPhone, that almost never happens.

scenes.visual: HOOK, a big picture change every 0.5 s. Frame 0: a giant thumb flicks a feed on a phone that fills the screen, already moving. 'One frame': time freezes, the feed splits into a film strip of frames flying past; one frame turns red and lags behind. '8 milliseconds': a frame-time graph slams in across the full width, green bars with one tall red spike, a drum counter rolls to 8 ms. 'can't see it': extreme macro of an eye, the red frame reflected, gone in a blink. 'thumb can feel it': macro of the fingertip on glass, a red shock ripple runs from the glass into the finger. 'On an iPhone': the graph flattens to a perfect green line and the phone redraws in titanium. 'never happens': the green line runs off screen like a heartbeat.

scenes.text: That is not luck. To make a scroll this smooth, Apple designed its own chips, its own modem and its own software, and spent 125 million dollars a day on research last year. So let's open it up, layer by layer, all the way down to a single transistor.

'chips / modem / software': three hero objects rise on lit pedestals one per word (A20 Pro package, C2 modem, a glass iOS layer stack). '125 million dollars a day': a mechanical drum counter rolls to $125,000,000 / DAY with a calendar flipping behind it; footnote 'Apple FY2026 R&D: $45.77 billion'. 'single transistor': continuous nano dive preview, board -> chip -> die -> one glowing transistor, then pulls back. Source credit on the counter shot.

scenes.text: Start with the screen. It can redraw 120 times a second. So every frame has a deadline: about 8.3 milliseconds. Miss it, and the old picture stays on screen for one more beat. Engineers call that a hitch.

hits.note: 120 Hz drum counter rolls
120 locks
ON TIME stamp on the first frame
the gate shuts: no new frame
LATE stamp
HITCH stamp (hero of the scene)

scenes.visual: World 'The deadline'. Macro of the OLED panel: red, green and blue sub-pixels in rows, lighting in waves. '120 times a second': a refresh scan line sweeps down again and again while a counter spins to 120 Hz. 'deadline': a long timeline with VSYNC gates every 8.3 ms, like finish lines; a frame card races to each gate and gets stamped ON TIME. 'Miss it': one frame card arrives late, the gate closes, the previous picture is copied into the slot (ghost duplicate) in red. 'hitch': the red slot gets a HITCH stamp and the scroll above visibly jerks once.

scenes.text: Here is the race. Your finger moves, and the touch goes to the app. The app works out what should change, then hands it over. A separate system process, the render server, prepares the frame. The graphics chip paints it. And the display shows it on the very next tick.

scenes.visual: World 'The render loop', one wide machine laid out left to right across the 16:9 frame, five stations joined by a glowing track: TOUCH (finger on glass, capacitive grid lights up) -> APP (a glass app window, layout boxes rearranging) -> RENDER SERVER (a separate dark tower, layer tree becomes a stack of tiles) -> GPU (a chip die, tiles painted into pixels) -> DISPLAY (panel lights). One frame packet travels the track; the camera follows it station by station as each is named, while an 8.3 ms deadline bar drains along the bottom of the machine. The packet lands at the display with time to spare: ON TIME. Labels follow Apple's own names: Event, Commit, Render prepare, Render execute, Display.

scenes.text: And here is the clever part. Animations run inside that render server, outside the app. So even when an app is busy, the motion on screen can keep going. And when nothing moves, ProMotion slows the screen right down to save battery.

(second half of the stuck double knock)

ProMotion dial needle winds down

scenes.visual: Same machine, pulled back into a split: the APP window on the left, the RENDER SERVER tower on the right, a glass wall between them. 'outside the app': an animation (a card springing open) is lifted out of the app and keeps playing inside the tower. 'app is busy': the app side goes amber, a spinner and a jammed gear, while the right side keeps animating smoothly, green frame ticks landing on time. 'ProMotion': a refresh dial; it swings to 120 Hz while a feed scrolls, then drops low as the feed stops and a battery fills. No floor number shown (Apple publishes none): the dial is labelled 'up to 120 Hz'.

scenes.text: But software alone cannot win that race 7,200 times a minute. It needs a chip built for exactly this software. And in 2008, Apple did not design a single one.

hits.note: portal into the tunnel of gates

7,200 locks

the empty socket: a question mark

scenes.visual: The deadline gates multiply into a tunnel of gates rushing at the camera, counter racing to 7,200 / MIN. 'a chip built for exactly this software': the glass iOS layer stack lowers onto a chip like a key into a lock, pins light up where they meet. '2008': hard change of world: the first iPhone era, an older rounded phone opens to show a board whose main chip is blank, an empty socket with a dashed outline and a question mark where Apple's own chip would be.

scenes.text: So it bought a small chip company, P.A. Semi, for 278 million dollars. Two years later came the A4, the first chip Apple designed itself. In 2013, the A7 became the first 64-bit chip in a phone. In 2017, the A11 added a Neural Engine for machine learning. And in 2020, the same idea, scaled up, became the M1, and replaced Intel inside the Mac.

scenes.visual: World 'The chip road': a long horizontal road of year markers 2008 -> 2020 that the camera travels along, one stop per sentence, each chip redrawn in code from real package photos and growing in size and detail. 2008: a signed deal card, drum counter $278,000,000. 2010: the A4 package drops into the empty socket from S06, the board lights. 2013: A7, its die x-rays to show registers widening from 32 to 64 lanes. 2017: A11, a new block on the die lights up as a small neural net, a face outline is recognised. 2020: the die scales up into the M1, a laptop opens around it and a blue chip is pushed out of the frame. Real photos on glass cards beside the redrawn chips where a licence allows (A4 package, M1 press image), each with a bottom-right source credit.

scenes.text: Then Apple went after the chips around it. Its own modem, the C1, in 2025. Its own wireless chip, the N1, the same year. And now, in the iPhone 18 Pro, the A20 Pro: Apple's first 2 nanometer chip.

scenes.visual: Same road, 2025 -> 2026, now on a modern logic board. Around the main chip two neighbouring chips with other makers' blank labels lift out and Apple-designed ones drop in: C1 (radio waves pulse out to a cell tower), N1 (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Thread rings). 'iPhone 18 Pro': the board slides into a titanium phone. 'A20 Pro': hero shot, the package fills the frame, laser-etched, light sweep; a short nano dive to a 2 nm nanosheet transistor and the label 'TSMC 2 nm'.

scenes.text: Eighteen years of work, for one feeling under your thumb. So where does all of it actually sit? Let's open the phone.

hits.note: 18 YEARS counter rolls

camera pushes inside the phone (hand-off to Act 2)

scenes.visual: The whole road 2008 -> 2026 folds up into the phone from the hook; the thumb returns and scrolls, the green frame line perfectly flat. 'where does it sit': an x-ray pass sweeps over the phone showing the board glowing inside. 'open the phone': the back glass lifts, screws spin out, and the camera pushes into the opening. End of Act 1 on the dive (Act 2 starts inside).
